Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small red sailboat with two cream-white sails on calm teal water at sunset, with the setting sun, its golden path on the water, and a violet mountain on the far shore.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

11 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: The red sailboat and its reflection, right of center (about 77% across, 60% down in the frame). Light: The setting sun, low and just left of center (48.5% across, 42.5% down in the frame), behind and to the left of the boat. Lit edges face left, toward the sun.How this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: laying in and blending the whole skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: filling the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: the mountainFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat: the shoreline stripFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: short dashes near the horizonRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • Liner (#1 or #0): the mast and boomLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Positions in the steps are percentages across and down: each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

STEP 1 OF 11

Paint the sunset sky

  1. The light comes from the sun, low and just left of center, behind the boat. Every highlight faces left, toward it.
  2. Violet across the top tenth, creamy, in long side-to-side strokes edge to edge.
  3. Sunset pink from 12% to 20% down, then Sunset orange from 22% down to about 57%, a little past the horizon line at 54%.
  4. Add a little Sunset pink into the orange at the far right, 44% to 54% down.
  5. Stroke back over each join while wet until the bands melt together, then stop. Below 57% stays white.
Build the depth, dark first
ValuePaintWhere
topSky violet0 to 10% down
middleSunset pink12 to 20% down, and a touch low on the right
bottomSunset orange22% down to about 57%, brightest around the sun's spot
Paints for this step3 paints, 3 new
  • Sky violet new4 parts white, 3 parts ultramarine, 1 part red
  • Sunset pink new3 parts white, 2 parts red, 1 part ultramarine
  • Sunset orange new1 part yellow, 1 part red, a touch of white

Colors dry a little darker, so test each mix on the palette edge first.

The picture's sky stops right at the horizon (54%); running yours to about 57% is fine, the water covers it.

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull the flat edge to edge in one level stroke, then go back over each join while it's wet.

Watch out: Don't stop the orange at the horizon: run it a little past, so the water overlaps it and no white peeks through.

Watch out: Overblending turns the bands muddy. A few strokes over each join, then stop.

Heads up, this picture is a little off: The sky in the picture stops at the horizon (54% down) instead of 58%, so it doesn't show the sky run past the horizon. Spotted while writing the text. Paint what the steps say.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 11

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. Center the sun 48% across and 42% down, about 3/4 inch wide. Trace a coin or bottle cap lightly first.
  3. Fill it with Sun yellow, creamy, in small circles from the middle out.
  4. Let it dry, then give it a second coat so no orange shows through.

Watch out: Light over orange needs two coats; one looks patchy and that's normal.

STEP 3 OF 11

Paint the far mountain and shoreline

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. Outline the mountain's top with the flat's corner: up from 45% down at the left edge to a rounded peak 12% across, 40% down, then down to the horizon at 43% across.
  3. Fill it with Mountain violet in short horizontal strokes, creamy.
  4. Pull a Shore navy strip from 50% to 54% down, edge to edge, under the mountain and on to the right.

STEP 4 OF 11

Paint the teal water

  1. Light teal, creamy, in long level strokes from the shoreline down to about 65%.
  2. Deep teal from the bottom edge up to about 75%.
  3. Blend where they meet, 65% to 75% down, with level strokes. No white left anywhere.

STEP 5 OF 11

Add ripples to the water

  1. Let the water dry. Try a few dashes on scrap paper first.
  2. Deep teal streaks in the lower half, level, 1 to 2 inches long.
  3. Light teal streaks over the whole water, a little whiter than in step 4 so they show: short and close near the horizon, longer and farther apart near the bottom.

Brushes

1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Horizontal dashes on water. Touch the edge of the flat down and slide it sideways a little, light pressure, then lift.

Watch out: Curved or tilted dashes make the water look like it's sloping. Every ripple is level.

Watch out: Midway the painting can look unfinished and odd. That's the ugly stage; keep going.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 11

Paint the sun's path on the water

  1. Let the water dry.
  2. Golden orange dashes straight down from the sun: short and close at the horizon, 43% to 54% across.
  3. Lower down, longer dashes spreading out to 30% to 64% across, with teal gaps between. Stop near the bottom edge.
  4. Let the orange dry, then Pale gold dashes down the middle of the path, over the orange.
  5. Add a few stray orange dashes on the left water, 8% to 23% across, 72% to 82% down.

STEP 7 OF 11

Paint the two sails

  1. Let the sky dry. Dot the three corners of each sail, then build them as in the diagram.
  2. Left sail: tip 80% across and 30% down, base along 57% down from 73% to 81% across.
  3. Right sail: tip 81% across, 27% down; base along 58% down from 81% to 90% across.
  4. Two coats of Sail white, drying between.
  5. Once the white is dry, two or three thin Sail shadow strokes down the middle of each sail with the #6 round, top to bottom.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A red sailboat on teal water at sunset, with the sun, its path, and a far violet mountain.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, or page around it.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape (an 11x14 hung sideways, following the 3:2 picture)

Done: crop

Left out: the left 7.5% (the foot of the mountain) and the right 7.5% (open water and sky right of the boat)

Why: Cropping to 14:11 loses 15% and keeps the boat, reflection, sun, and path whole. fit-canvas split the cut evenly, 7.5% off each side.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things, no textures made of hundreds of items, no detail inside big shapes beyond dashes, and about 7 parts (under the budget of 8).

Why: Already beginner-sized.

Already a simple painting: a sunset sky in three bands, one far mountain, flat teal water, a golden sun path, and one small red sailboat with its reflection. The hard parts for a beginner are a clean gradient, keeping the water level, and getting the boat's proportions right; the rest is repeated dashes.

Subject: A small red sailboat with two cream-white sails on calm teal water at sunset, with the setting sun, its golden path on the water, and a violet mountain on the far shore.
Focal point: The red sailboat and its reflection, right of center (about 77% across, 60% down in the frame).
Light: The setting sun, low and just left of center (48.5% across, 42.5% down in the frame), behind and to the left of the boat. Lit edges face left, toward the sun.

Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

The owner named acrylic-paint-along-beginner.

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

A back-to-front landscape with a sky, far land, water, and one subject on top is exactly what the paint-along technique teaches.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

How the paint recipes were worked out15 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

  • Sky violet Delta E 5.0
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 3 parts ultramarine, 1 part red

    Written by eye first: 4 parts white, 2 parts ultramarine blue, 1 part red

  • Sunset pink Delta E 6.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 2 parts red, 1 part ultramarine

    Written by eye first: 4 parts white, 2 parts red, a touch of blue

  • Sunset orange Delta E 1.7
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part yellow, 1 part red, a touch of white

    Written by eye first: 3 parts yellow, 2 parts red, a little white

  • Sun yellow Delta E 1.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 1 part red

    Written by eye first: 4 parts white, 2 parts yellow, a touch of red

  • Mountain violet Delta E 3.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

Why the steps go in this order11 steps

Back to front: sky, sun, far land, water, ripples, sun path, then the boat from back to front (sails, hull over their base, then the thin mast and boom over both), the reflection under it, and the brightest touches last.

  1. 1. Paint the sunset sky

    The farthest layer and the biggest area, run past the horizon so the water overlaps it.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    Its own small step so it can get two coats over the dry orange.

  3. 3. Paint the far mountain and shoreline

    The farthest land, over the dry sky, before the water meets it.

  4. 4. Paint the teal water

    Covers the rest of the canvas so no white is left before any marks go on top.

  5. 5. Add ripples to the water

    One kind of mark, split from the base so the base can dry first.

  6. 6. Paint the sun's path on the water

    Sits on top of the ripples and lines up with the sun.

  7. 7. Paint the two sails

    The boat's back pieces, over the sky and shoreline.

  8. 8. Paint the red hull

    Overlaps the sails' base, so it goes after them.

  9. 9. Paint the mast and boom

    Thin liner lines over the dry sails and hull, last on the boat.

  10. 10. Paint the boat's reflection

    Mirrors the finished boat, so it waits until the boat is done.

  11. 11. Add the brightest highlights

    The brightest touches go last.

Where Claude drew diagrams2 steps, free

The sails and hull are shaped objects whose proportions decide whether the boat looks right, so both got construction diagrams; everything else is a gradient, a flat shape, or a repeated level dash.

  • Step 7: Paint the two sails beginner check, and the step review (6b) found the text pointing at a diagram that didn't exist yet

    Noticed: A shaped object appearing whole in one step, two triangles of different heights meeting on one line.

    Pieces: Dot the three corners of each sail, then the left (shorter, thinner) triangle, then the right (taller, wider) one, then the fold strokes once dry, the way a teacher would start from the corners.

  • Step 8: Paint the red hull beginner check

    Noticed: The hull's raised left point and sloped top were misread in an earlier sailboat run, and a flat box is the likely beginner mistake.

    Pieces: One top-edge line from the raised left tip down to the right, then the fill to a curved bottom, then the dark red band, with the sails shown as done.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • lock-steps (tool): the backward pass copies the finish wherever no later step paints, but inside later steps' boxes each step keeps its own render, so the render's slightly different sky or water shade shows as straight-edged rectangles (the sails' box in the sky of steps 1-2, the path and reflection boxes in the water of steps 5-9). The 6b reviewer flagged two of them as drift. A low-frequency color match of each render to the finish before locking fixed the sky here (filters/tone_match.py, try 1), but bled object ghosts into bare water; the tool could match tones only where both show the same background, or feather the backward pass far wider than 4 px.
  • mix (tool): Light teal and Deep teal both solved to the same recipe (3 ultramarine, 1 yellow, 1 white) because neither teal is reachable and both clamp to the nearest mix. Nothing warned about two paints sharing a recipe; the 6b reviewer caught it. Moving Light teal's sample spot to a lighter streak separated them. mix could flag paints whose recipes come out identical.
  • Renders stop the sky at the horizon even when looks_like asks for a straight edge 4% below it (58% asked, 54% painted). The text now says to run past it; this is the third run with the same failure.
  • Every step render after the sun path copied the path's pale gold middle from the finish, so a highlights step can't hold back colors the finish shows in an area an earlier step paints. Plan highlights only for marks that sit where no earlier step paints, or accept they show early.
  • The research has no stroke result for the sun-path and reflection dashes beyond the YAML's 'Horizontal dashes on water'; nothing on the order of a reflection (colors, then the liner line once dry).
  • fit-canvas now splits a crop evenly when the subject fits either way, and uses the photo itself as the frame when its shape matches, so no band render was needed (both learned on the last sailboat run).
